description: A team of curious minds, creative thinkers, and problem-solvers who turn ideas into reality.
summary:
Earth Songbook is an interactive web-based “Earth Jukebox” where every NASA Earth Information Center visualization has its own song. Visitors drop the needle on a retro record, choose one of eight visualizations (carbon dioxide, ocean currents, lightning, rain and snow, forests, aerosols, aurora), and hear the picture. In real time, a sweeping line reads each frame: height sets pitch, colour sets the note or instrument, left-right sets stereo position, and a heartbeat pulses only when the picture changes. For records with a NASA colour bar, colours are decoded into approximate values such as ppm or temperature. All sound is synthesized live in the browser, using musical scales so it stays pleasant to hear.

Accessibility is central: spoken frame descriptions, full keyboard and screen reader support, a Detector to listen to one colour or area, pre-recorded samples, and the option to use your own images. It matters because Earth science shouldn’t depend on sight alone, and because listening can reach the heart, helping people feel connected to our changing planet. It is an artistic, accessible way to listen to the pictures, not a scientific measurement tool.
details:
What it does: Earth Songbook is a web-based Earth Jukebox. Pick one of eight NASA visualizations (CO₂, ocean currents, lightning, rain and snow, forests, aerosols, aurora) and hear it as live music. A sweeping line reads each frame: height sets pitch, colour sets the note or instrument, and left-right sets stereo position. Chords follow the light, and a heartbeat sounds only when the picture changes. For records with a colour bar, we use NASA Earth Information Center’s own colour bar as the reference: each colour (for example, blue for cold and red for warm in temperature) is matched to its approximate value (ppm, °C, mm/hour) and translated into a musical note.

Benefits and impact: Blind and low-vision users can experience Earth science, with spoken frame descriptions, full keyboard and screen reader support, and a Detector to listen to one colour or area. The aim is to make people feel connected to the planet, not just informed.

Tools: HTML, CSS and JavaScript in one file. Web Audio API (all sound synthesized live), Canvas, SVG, MediaRecorder and SpeechSynthesis. No special hardware.

Creative: A retro vinyl jukebox, with a different musical character per record: a breath-like arpeggio for CO₂, a waltz for the sea, a slow echoing song for the aurora. Listeners can also choose the instrument (piano, guitar, saxophone or drums), each with its own animated background.

Considered: Accessibility first, and musical rules so the sound stays pleasant. We were open about limits: colour-bar values are approximate readings of NASA’s legends, and this is an artistic tool, not a scientific instrument. NASA does not endorse it.

Responsible AI Use and Scientific Verification: AI (Claude) was used to speed up learning and development, not to replace scientific reasoning or independent evaluation. Our team reviewed the generated code, tested the application, and checked scientific interpretations against NASA sources, including the NASA Scientific Visualization Studio and the Earth Information Center. AI-assisted code and data contributions are acknowledged in the project documentation, and any AI-generated visual or audio materials in the final submission are identified according to NASA Space Apps Challenge requirements.
